title: Lloyds launches Investing in Britain Hub
short: Lloyds has introduced a new online hub to provide customers with information on UK companies and sectors as part of a diversified investment approach.
quick: Lloyds has introduced a new online hub to provide customers with information on UK companies and sectors as part of a diversified investment approach.
lead: Lloyds says it has launched the Investing in Britain Hub to give customers information about investing in UK companies and sectors as part of a diversified investment approach. The online resource brings together details on various UK investment themes to help customers understand how UK-listed companies and domestic growth opportunities fit into a diversified portfolio. The hub is available to Lloyds customers as an online resource.
blocks: Lloyds says it has launched the Investing in Britain Hub to give customers information about investing in UK companies and sectors as part of a diversified investment approach. The online resource brings together details on various UK investment themes to help customers understand how UK-listed companies and domestic growth opportunities fit into a diversified portfolio. The hub is available to Lloyds customers as an online resource.

The hub forms part of the broader Investing in Britain initiative led by The Investment Association. This wider campaign was launched by The Investment Association in partnership with member firms across the UK investment management industry to improve awareness of UK investment opportunities and help people engage with long-term investing. Through dedicated online hubs, participating firms provide educational content and resources to help customers understand opportunities in UK businesses and the role investing plays in economic growth.

Manuel Pardavila-Gonzalez, Managing Director for Investments at Lloyds Banking Group, says helping people build long-term financial resilience is central to their operations and that the hub offers customers a simple way to learn about opportunities in UK companies. Lloyds says the resource has been designed to make it easier for customers to access UK market information and explore investment opportunities available through Lloyds products and services, reflecting the firm's commitment to improving financial confidence and supporting informed decision-making.

title: UK financial complaints rise to 1.85 million as firms pay £240 million in redress
short: The FCA reports a 6.3% rise in complaints for the first half of 2026. Current accounts remain the most complained-about product, and 54.8% of closed complaints were upheld.
quick: Financial firms reported 1.85 million complaints in January–June 2026, up 6.3% on the previous half-year. The FCA also reports £240 million paid in redress.
lead: UK financial-services firms received 1.85 million complaints in the first six months of 2026, up 6.3% on the previous half-year, according to new figures from the Financial Conduct Authority.
blocks: Complaints are up, with current accounts leading

UK financial-services firms received 1.85 million complaints between January and June 2026, up 6.3% from the previous six months, when firms reported 1.74 million. The figures, published by the Financial Conduct Authority on 22 October, cover complaints across banking, insurance, investments, pensions and home finance.

Current accounts remained the most complained-about individual product. But that ranking is based on the number of complaints, not the rate of complaints per customer or account. The FCA's aggregate figures draw on returns from more than 3,000 regulated firms.
What the upheld figure actually means

The FCA says firms upheld 1,003,011 complaints, representing 54.8% of complaints closed during the period. That distinction matters: the proportion is not calculated against the 1.85 million new complaints received.

An upheld complaint is one the firm agrees with, either fully or partly. Separately, the FCA reports that firms paid consumers £240 million in redress. The amount paid and the percentage of complaints upheld are different measures; neither should be used as a substitute for the other.

The regulator reports that 44.8% of complaints were closed within three days. A further 49.7% were closed after three days but within eight weeks, meaning 94.5% were closed within eight weeks in total. The remaining 5.5% took longer.

For customer-service and complaints teams, this adds an important second dimension to the headline volume: it shows how long firms took to bring complaints to an outcome, alongside the number they received.
What the figures can — and cannot — tell us

More complaints do not automatically mean a firm delivers poorer service. A larger bank or insurer may naturally receive more complaints simply because it serves more people or has more accounts and policies. The FCA says readers should consider a firm's size, uphold rates, resolution times and redress rather than judging performance on complaint totals alone.

There are also limits to the dataset. The published aggregate totals exclude complaints from firms authorised only for consumer-credit activities. The more detailed firm-level disclosures concentrate on firms meeting the FCA's reporting thresholds, while historic figures can change when firms correct their returns.

For anyone comparing providers, the useful question is not just who received the most complaints, but what happened to those complaints and how the numbers relate to the size of the business.
glossary: A complaint the firm agrees with, in full or in part.
Steps taken to put a problem right; the FCA's £240 million figure relates to redress payments.
Complaints figures combined across reporting firms, rather than figures for one firm alone.
